summary:
The legal position a trans visitor meets in Austria is broadly permissive. Sex between men was decriminalised in 1971, marriage has been open to same-sex couples since 2017, and full adoption rights have applied since 2016. A trans visitor travelling with a partner in what Austrian law would classify as a same-sex relationship therefore stands inside the ordinary marriage and family framework rather than outside it.

Legal gender recognition is possible without mandatory medical procedures, and Austrian documents may carry an 'X', indeterminate, or no gender marker; intersex people may choose 'diverse', 'inter', or no designation. The third-gender option dates from a June 2018 Constitutional Court ruling that gender identity must be accurately reflected in official documents, with the first non-binary passport and 'divers' birth certificate issued in May 2019; the Interior Ministry restricted 'divers' to holders of a medical panel certificate of intersexuality. Changing legal gender and name does not require prior sex-reassignment surgery, but is conditional on submitting a psychiatric opinion, and public health insurance payment for sex-change treatment is likewise bound on psychiatric opinions.

The Equal Treatment Act has prohibited employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2004. Recent amendments broaden its use of "gender" to cover gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics; gender identity and intersex status have no separate listing and are handled under that term. Since January 2017 every federal state has extended anti-discrimination protection to goods and services, Lower Austria being the last to do so. From 1 January 2016 hate speech based on sexual orientation is banned, and crimes committed on that ground are treated as an aggravating factor. The 1993 Security Police Act obliges police to avoid actions perceived as biased on sexual-orientation grounds.

Austria's hate-crime recording for 2025 counted 6,751 suspected hate crimes, 7,327 prejudice motives and 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence, with police data acknowledging under-recording. Official statistics for that reporting year show homophobic offences rising while transphobic incidents declined. In March 2025 police arrested 15 people, aged 14 to 26, over a wave of hate attacks in which at least 17 LGBTQ people were lured via fake dating-platform accounts to remote locations, ambushed by masked groups, filmed, and falsely accused of being paedophiles; investigators believe the real victim count is much higher. The same neo-Nazi network was uncovered in March using fake dating profiles to ambush gay and bisexual men. The most recent documented incident in this record is from March 2025; no later instance is documented.

Transgender people have been allowed to serve openly in the Austrian Armed Forces since 2014, and LGBT people serve openly generally. A Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report (2025) sets out the legal framework governing LGBTIQ people in Austrian prisons, including gender self-determination and anti-discrimination protection in detention; the Justice Ministry's answer to parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 (May-June 2025) is the official source on housing transgender people in penal institutions and is in German. Ombud guidance addresses gender-inclusive forms for intersex and non-binary people.

Puberty blockers for youth experiencing gender dysphoria have been endorsed by the Austrian Society of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (ÖGKJP) and the Austrian Society of Gynecology and Obstetrics (OEGGG). Lesbian couples can access artificial insemination and IVF. Parliament passed a non-binding resolution on 2 July 2019 calling for a government bill banning conversion therapy on minors, with all parties voting in favour; TeenSTAR, found in 2018 offering minors conversion-therapy classes, was banned in April 2019 after the Education Directorate Salzburg suspended its workshops. In September 2024 the far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) won the most votes in a national election for the first time since WWII (29.2%), raising concerns about what an FPÖ-led government could mean for LGBTQ+ people.
tangentialFactors:
Austria recorded 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 7,327 prejudice motives in 2025, with 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence; police data acknowledges under-recording, and the ranking of offences by raw count reflects population size rather than per-capita risk.

The FPÖ's 29.2% first-place result in the September 2024 national election is the clearest indicator of political turbulence for LGBTQ+ people; the ÖVP and FPÖ have historically opposed LGBT rights. Public opinion as of 2023 showed 65% support for same-sex marriage and 66% agreeing nothing is wrong with a same-sex relationship.

New Ministry of Education rules restrict outside sex-education providers, and a Vienna petition for queer sauna time slots was rejected, both documented in the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 covering 2025.
localsOnly:
Trans Austrians can change legal gender and name without prior sex-reassignment surgery, but the change is conditional on submitting a psychiatric opinion; public health insurance payment for sex-change treatment is likewise bound on psychiatric opinions.

The Interior Ministry restricts the 'divers' birth-certificate marker to people holding a medical panel certificate of intersexuality, even though the Constitutional Court's June 2018 ruling requires gender identity to be accurately reflected in documents.

Anti-discrimination protection in goods and services exists at Land level in all nine federal states since January 2017, with Lower Austria the last to adopt it; the Equal Treatment Act's "gender" wording carries gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics without separate listing.

As of July 2020 no expungement or compensation scheme had been implemented for historical convictions, including lesbianism criminalised after the Anschluss and 1940 court alignment to Paragraph 175.

Community infrastructure operates openly, including HOSI Wien (founded 1979), HOSI Salzburg, ALGF and Afro Rainbow Austria, with groups in Vienna, Linz, Innsbruck, Salzburg and Graz and an annual Vienna Gay Pride/Regenbogenparade.
outOfScopeNotes:
The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 also documents a rejected Vienna petition for queer sauna time slots and new Ministry of Education rules restricting outside sex-education providers; these are adjacent policy items rather than direct visitor-risk findings.

The DW report and the ILGA-Europe review describe the same March 2025 dating-app ambush network; whether the 15 arrests produced convictions is not sourced here.

The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute report and the Justice Ministry answer to parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 are the cited authorities on detention of trans people, but their specific operative rules are not reproduced in this inventory; the Justice Ministry answer is in German.

The claim that legal gender recognition requires no mandatory medical procedures sits alongside the psychiatric-opinion requirement for name and gender change; how these interact in current practice is not resolved by the sources.

Whether conversion therapy on minors has been formally banned by statute, as opposed to the 2 July 2019 non-binding parliamentary resolution and the April 2019 TeenSTAR ban, is not sourced here.
